title: 3-Read Friday #124
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's weekly roundup curates three blog posts on the teaching profession and classroom practice, each introduced with his own brief commentary. He opens with Paul Kirschner and Nidhi Sachdeva's argument that years of service are too easily confused with expertise, which they locate at the intersection of science and craft and which must be developed deliberately. He then presents David Didau's qualified case for copying, noting his own opposition to copying notes while crediting Didau's distinction between transcription and mimicry. The third pick is Adam Boxer's post on FLMOP, which Barton frames as evidence that classroom hubbub often stems from the order in which instructions are given. Together the selections sketch a practical view of expertise as something built through deliberate attention to small, evidence-informed routines.
points: Kirschner and Sachdeva argue that time served in classrooms is not the same as expertise, which must be developed deliberately at the meeting point of science and craft.
Barton, who opposes students copying notes and worked examples, highlights Didau's distinction between mindless transcription and purposeful mimicry.
Boxer's FLMOP post is presented as a small change to instruction order that can markedly reduce low-level classroom noise.
The roundup pairs a big-picture argument about professional expertise with two concrete classroom routines.
quotes: Paul and Nidhi argue that we have spent far too long confusing time served with expertise.
Real expertise, they argue, sits at the intersection of science and craft, and it has to be developed far more deliberately than we currently allow.
In this post, David agrees that copying from the board is a very poor proxy for learning, because students barely have to think about what they’re writing.
But he then argues that transcription and mimicry are not the same thing, and makes a compelling case for when copying genuinely earns its place, and what has to happen next for it to count.
Adam argues that much of the low-level hubbub in our classrooms comes not from what our instructions say, but from the order in which we say it.
One tiny tweak, illustrated with some brilliant classroom footage, can make a surprisingly big difference to calm and focus.
